title: How Search Models and Queries Work
readerIntent: Understand search-model resolution, query execution, consistency, cache, and tenant boundaries.
summary: A search operation resolves tenant, module, schema, and index context before dispatching a normalized operation through the configured provider pipeline.

sections.heading: Runtime flow
items: A secured API, service, import process, or internal workflow requests a search operation.
Nodics resolves the active tenant, owning module, schema model, and index name.
The provider-neutral service obtains the active search model.
The operation is dispatched through its search pipeline.
The configured adapter maps the operation to engine-specific behavior.
Eligible results use the centralized cacheability policy.
Failures return through normalized SearchError handling.

sections.heading: Supported normalized operations
items: Health, refresh, exists, get, and search.
Save, bulk, update, remove, and remove by query.
Get or update schema mappings.
Create, execute, or remove an index.

sections.heading: Consistency
paragraphs: Search is normally a derived view of authoritative records. Each capability must state whether indexing is synchronous or eventually consistent, how lag is detected, and whether a bounded permission-safe database fallback is supported.

sections.heading: Index identity and isolation
paragraphs: Index naming and aliases derive from governed tenant, module, schema, version, and environment context. A browser does not submit an arbitrary physical index name.
Shared and dedicated indexes both preserve isolation. Provider credentials and aliases are configuration, while the business module owns searchable meaning.

sections.heading: Query contract
items: Allowed fields, operators, filters, sorting, pagination, and aggregation are explicit.
Unknown fields and unbounded query shapes are rejected.
Authorization and tenant filters cannot be removed by client input.
Stable record identifiers allow authoritative retrieval after discovery.
Highlighting and display fields exclude secrets and protected content.

sections.heading: Indexing lifecycle
items: Create or update mappings from the effective search model.
Index after authoritative create and update.
Remove or tombstone after authoritative lifecycle change.
Coordinate bulk import, publishing, migration, and reindexing.
Detect lag, rejected documents, mapping conflicts, and drift.
Rebuild safely without mixing environments or tenants.

sections.heading: Cache interaction
paragraphs: Search-result caching follows centralized cacheability policy. Cache keys include every scope that changes authorization or result meaning. Mutations, publishing, and index changes invalidate or expire eligible entries.
Cache never repairs a stale index and cannot broaden result visibility.

sections.heading: Provider outage behavior
paragraphs: The capability defines whether a query fails, returns a bounded stale result, or uses a permission-safe database fallback. Fallback is not automatic because an unrestricted database query can change semantics or overload persistence.
Indexing failures enter retry or reconciliation with observable lag. Authoritative data remains valid even while its search projection is degraded.

sections.heading: Example: BackOffice model search
paragraphs: An employee searches for Tenant by code and description. BackOffice discovers the authorized Tenant contract; Search resolves the Profile-owned model and tenant context and returns friendly results.
The employee selects a result, then Profile reads or updates the item authoritatively. A missing result can lead to authorized nested creation, not direct insertion into the index.

sections.heading: Operational evidence
items: Query latency, error rate, timeouts, and rejected complexity.
Indexing throughput, lag, retry queue, and rejected documents.
Mapping and alias versions, health, shard or provider capacity.
Tenant-isolation and permission-denial tests.
Reindex, import finalization, publishing, backup, and recovery results.
